direction_contract.statement: The canonical, normally stated conjecture or positive resolution target.
direction_contract.prove: The worker is asked to establish the canonical statement.
direction_contract.disprove: The worker is asked to refute the canonical statement; the prompt records the appropriate counterexample, construction, or contrary theorem.

review_policy.terminal_resolution: Only an unconditional proof or disproof of the canonical statement may set the problem to Solved, settle the opposite direction as false, trigger the solved-donor acknowledgment, or sweep the pools. An assumption written into the canonical statement is part of the statement and does not make a result conditional.
review_policy.conditional_result: A result that depends on assumptions absent from the canonical statement must name every assumption in the admin review note. It is recorded and displayed as 'Resolved under assumption: X; unconditional problem remains open,' but it is non-terminal: the problem returns to Open, the opposite direction is not settled false, and no solved-problem sweep or solved-donor acknowledgment occurs.

problems.title: The Riemann Hypothesis
problems.statement: Every non-trivial zero of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) = Σ n⁻ˢ (analytically continued) has real part exactly 1/2.

directions.disprove: Exhibit (or prove the existence of) a zero ρ with Re(ρ) ≠ 1/2. This is disprovable-in-principle by a finite computation: a zero off the line can be certified rigorously by interval arithmetic (argument-principle counts in a box).

problems.title: The Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH)
problems.statement: Every non-trivial zero of every Dirichlet L-function L(s, χ) has real part 1/2.

directions.disprove: A single off-line zero of a single L-function disproves GRH. The most-discussed candidate type is a **Siegel zero**: a real zero of L(s, χ) for a real character χ, very close to s = 1. This is a *simple* potential counterexample — one real number.

problems.title: Goldbach's Conjecture
problems.statement: Every even integer n ≥ 4 is the sum of two primes.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one even number with no representation. Finite certificate: check all primes p ≤ n/2 and confirm n − p is composite each time.

problems.title: The Twin Prime Conjecture
problems.statement: There are infinitely many primes p with p + 2 also prime.

directions.disprove: Prove there is a *largest* twin prime pair. **This cannot be done by exhibiting a finite object** — no computation can disprove an infinitude statement. The contrarian direction is a finiteness theorem.

problems.title: Legendre's Conjecture
problems.statement: For every positive integer n there is a prime p with n² < p < (n+1)².

directions.disprove: Exhibit an n with no prime between n² and (n+1)². Finite certificate: a primality check of ~2n numbers.

problems.title: Landau's Problem: Primes of the Form n² + 1
problems.statement: There are infinitely many primes of the form n² + 1. (Special case of the Bunyakovsky/Schinzel Hypothesis H family.)

directions.disprove: Prove only finitely many n² + 1 are prime. Again **no finite certificate is possible**; this direction requires a theorem.

problems.title: The Collatz (3n + 1) Conjecture
problems.statement: Define T(n) = n/2 for even n, 3n + 1 for odd n. For every positive integer n, iteration of T eventually reaches 1.

directions.disprove: Two distinct finite-or-semifinite disproof types: (a) a **non-trivial cycle** — finite certificate, just list the cycle; (b) a **divergent trajectory** — no finite certificate; divergence would itself need proof.

problems.title: The abc Conjecture
problems.statement: For every ε > 0, there are only finitely many triples of coprime positive integers with a + b = c and c > rad(abc)^{1+ε}, where rad is the product of distinct prime divisors.

directions.disprove: Exhibit, for some fixed ε > 0, an **infinite family** of coprime triples with c > rad(abc)^{1+ε}. **No single triple can disprove abc** — the statement is "finitely many," so any one high-quality triple is consistent with it. This is a proof-required disproof (though an explicit parameterized family with a verified quality bound would do it).

problems.title: Odd Perfect Numbers
problems.statement: No odd perfect number exists (n is perfect if σ(n) = 2n).

directions.disprove: Exhibit one odd perfect number — a clean finite certificate.

problems.title: Infinitude of Mersenne Primes
problems.statement: There are infinitely many primes of the form 2ᵖ − 1.

directions.disprove: Prove there is a largest Mersenne prime. **No finite certificate possible.** Delightfully, the mirror problem is *also* open: it is not proved that infinitely many 2ᵖ − 1 (p prime) are *composite*. A contrarian could aim at either.

problems.title: Fermat Primes
problems.statement: The only Fermat primes are F₀ = 3, F₁ = 5, F₂ = 17, F₃ = 257, and F₄ = 65537.

directions.disprove: Exhibit a sixth Fermat prime. Finite certificate (a Pépin test run, independently checkable).

problems.title: Beal's Conjecture
problems.statement: If Aˣ + Bʸ = Cᶻ with A, B, C positive integers, x, y, z integers ≥ 3, then A, B, C share a common prime factor.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one coprime solution — a finite certificate anyone can verify by arithmetic.

problems.title: The Erdős–Straus Conjecture
problems.statement: For every integer n ≥ 2, the equation 4/n = 1/x + 1/y + 1/z has a solution in positive integers x, y, z.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one n with no solution. Disproof is finitely certifiable in principle (solvability for fixed n reduces to a bounded search), though the certificate is a completeness argument, not one identity.

problems.title: Sums of Three Cubes
problems.statement: Every integer k with k ≢ ±4 (mod 9) is expressible as x³ + y³ + z³ for some integers x, y, and z.

directions.disprove: Prove some admissible k has no representation. **No finite certificate exists** — the search space is infinite, so a non-representability proof needs new theory (there is currently *no known obstruction* beyond the mod-9 one; proving any new obstruction would itself be a breakthrough).

problems.title: Brocard's Problem
problems.statement: The only solutions of n! + 1 = m² are (n, m) = (4, 5), (5, 11), (7, 71).

directions.disprove: Exhibit a fourth solution — a one-line finite certificate.

problems.title: The Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer Conjecture
problems.statement: For an elliptic curve E over ℚ, the algebraic rank of E(ℚ) equals the order of vanishing of L(E, s) at s = 1 (and the leading Taylor coefficient is given by the precise BSD formula involving Ш, regulator, Tamagawa numbers, torsion).

directions.disprove: Exhibit a curve where analytic rank ≠ algebraic rank, or where the leading-coefficient formula fails numerically in a certifiable way.

problems.title: The Littlewood Conjecture
problems.statement: For all real α, β: lim inf_{n→∞} n · ‖nα‖ · ‖nβ‖ = 0, where ‖·‖ is distance to the nearest integer.

directions.disprove: Exhibit a specific pair (α, β) with lim inf > 0 — e.g., prove the natural candidate pair (√2, √3) fails. A disproof requires a lower-bound proof for one pair (no finite certificate).

problems.title: Normality of π
problems.statement: π is normal in every base: each block of k digits occurs with limiting frequency b⁻ᵏ.

directions.disprove: Prove any digit-frequency anomaly — even something as weak as "the digit 7 occurs only finitely often in the decimal expansion of π" would be a shattering disproof. **Nothing known excludes this.** It is a genuinely open possibility, consistent with every proved theorem, that π's decimal expansion is eventually all 0s and 1s.

problems.title: Irrationality of the Euler–Mascheroni Constant γ
problems.statement: The Euler–Mascheroni constant γ is irrational.

directions.disprove: Prove γ = p/q for specific integers — a finite certificate (with a proof of the identity).

problems.title: Schanuel's Conjecture
problems.statement: If z₁, …, zₙ ∈ ℂ are linearly independent over ℚ, then the field ℚ(z₁, …, zₙ, e^{z₁}, …, e^{zₙ}) has transcendence degree ≥ n over ℚ.

directions.disprove: Exhibit an unexpected algebraic relation — the most famous concrete instances being: prove e + π is rational, or e·π is rational, or e and π are algebraically dependent. Each of these is open and none is excluded by any theorem. (It *is* known that e + π and e·π cannot both be rational — since e, π would then be algebraic — so a contrarian can have at most one of those two.)

problems.title: The Perfect Cuboid Problem
problems.statement: There is no rectangular box with all of: integer edge lengths a, b, c; integer face diagonals √(a²+b²), √(b²+c²), √(a²+c²); and integer space diagonal √(a²+b²+c²).

directions.disprove: Exhibit one — seven integers, instantly checkable.

problems.title: Navier–Stokes Existence and Smoothness (Clay problem)
problems.statement: Every smooth, divergence-free, rapidly decaying or periodic initial datum for the three-dimensional incompressible Navier–Stokes equations gives rise to a solution that remains smooth for all time.

directions.disprove: Construct initial data whose solution develops a singularity in finite time. This is widely considered a live possibility, not a fringe one.

problems.title: The Kakeya Conjecture in Dimensions ≥ 4
problems.statement: Every Kakeya set (a compact set in ℝⁿ containing a unit line segment in every direction) has Hausdorff dimension n.

directions.disprove: Construct a Kakeya set in some ℝⁿ, n ≥ 4, of Hausdorff dimension < n.

problems.title: The Invariant Subspace Problem (Hilbert space)
problems.statement: Every bounded linear operator on an infinite-dimensional separable complex Hilbert space has a non-trivial closed invariant subspace.

directions.disprove: Construct a Hilbert-space operator with no non-trivial closed invariant subspace.

problems.title: Sendov's Conjecture
problems.statement: If all n ≥ 2 zeros of a complex polynomial lie in the closed unit disk, then within distance 1 of each zero there is a zero of the derivative.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one polynomial and one root violating the bound — a finite certificate (algebraic numbers, verifiable exactly).

problems.title: Crouzeix's Conjecture
problems.statement: For every square complex matrix A and every polynomial p: ‖p(A)‖ ≤ 2·max{|p(z)| : z ∈ W(A)}, where W(A) is the numerical range (field of values) of A.

directions.disprove: Exhibit a matrix and polynomial with ratio > 2 — a finite certificate (numerical, but rigorously certifiable with interval arithmetic).

problems.title: The Inscribed Square Problem (Toeplitz, 1911)
problems.statement: Every Jordan curve (continuous simple closed curve) in the plane contains four points forming a square.

directions.disprove: Construct one Jordan curve with no inscribed square.

problems.title: The Union-Closed Sets Conjecture (Frankl)
problems.statement: Every finite union-closed family of sets (closed under pairwise union) other than {∅} has an element belonging to at least half of the sets.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one finite family where every element is in fewer than half the sets — a finite certificate.

problems.title: Hadwiger's Conjecture
problems.statement: For every t ≥ 1, every graph with no Kₜ minor is properly (t−1)-colorable.

directions.disprove: Exhibit a graph with no Kₜ minor and chromatic number ≥ t — a finite certificate (though certifying "no Kₜ minor" and "χ ≥ t" are both expensive computations, they are finite).

problems.title: The Reconstruction Conjecture (Kelly–Ulam)
problems.statement: Every finite simple graph on ≥ 3 vertices is determined up to isomorphism by its deck: the multiset of vertex-deleted subgraphs.

directions.disprove: Exhibit two non-isomorphic graphs with identical decks — a finite certificate.

problems.title: The Graceful Tree Conjecture (Ringel–Kotzig)
problems.statement: Every tree on n vertices has a graceful labeling: an injection of vertex labels into {0, …, n−1} such that edge labels |f(u) − f(v)| are exactly {1, …, n−1}.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one tree with no graceful labeling — finitely certifiable (exhaustive search over labelings).

problems.title: The Lonely Runner Conjecture
problems.statement: For k runners on a unit circle with distinct constant speeds, each runner is at some time at circular distance ≥ 1/k from every other runner (equivalently, in the standard reduction: for any k−1 nonzero integer speeds, there is a time t with all speeds' positions ‖vᵢt‖ ≥ 1/k).

directions.disprove: Exhibit a speed vector for which some runner is never lonely. Because of the integer reduction plus known bounds, a counterexample for fixed k is finitely certifiable in principle.

problems.title: The Hadwiger–Nelson Problem (Chromatic Number of the Plane)
problems.statement: In ZFC, the chromatic number of the Euclidean plane is 5.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical statement by combining the known lower bound with an explicit valid 5-coloring of the plane.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving that the plane requires at least 6 colors, for example through a finite 6-chromatic unit-distance graph.

problems.title: The Sunflower Conjecture (Erdős–Rado)
problems.statement: There is a constant C such that any family of more than Cʷ sets, each of size w, contains a 3-sunflower (three sets whose pairwise intersections all equal the common intersection).

directions.disprove: Construct, for every constant C, families of w-sets larger than Cʷ with no 3-sunflower. **No single finite family disproves the conjecture** — a disproof needs an infinite sequence of constructions beating every exponential base (proof-required, though an explicit construction family would do it).

problems.title: The Erdős–Szekeres Conjecture (Happy Ending problem, exact version)
problems.statement: For every n ≥ 3, any set of 2^{n−2} + 1 points in the plane in general position contains n points in convex position — and this is sharp.

directions.disprove: Two directions: (a) exhibit a configuration of 2^{n−2} + 1 points with no convex n-gon for some n (disproving the sufficiency) — for n = 7 this is just **33 points**, a strikingly small potential certificate; (b) improve the upper bound below 2^{n−2}+1 for some n, disproving sharpness of the known lower-bound constructions.

problems.title: The Cycle Double Cover Conjecture
problems.statement: Every bridgeless finite graph has a family of cycles such that every edge lies in exactly two of them.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one bridgeless graph with no cycle double cover — a finite certificate (verification is a finite, if expensive, search).

problems.title: The Erdős Conjecture on Arithmetic Progressions
problems.statement: If A ⊆ ℕ has Σ_{a∈A} 1/a = ∞, then A contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length.

directions.disprove: Construct a set with divergent reciprocal sum containing no k-term AP for some k. This would be an explicit construction plus two proofs (divergence; AP-freeness) — no single finite certificate.

problems.title: The Missing Moore Graph (degree 57)
problems.statement: A Moore graph of degree 57 exists; equivalently, there is a 57-regular graph on 3250 vertices with girth 5.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical statement by constructing such a graph and verifying its parameters.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving that no Moore graph of degree 57 exists.

problems.title: The Hadamard Conjecture
problems.statement: A Hadamard matrix (±1 entries, HHᵀ = nI) exists for every order n = 4k.

directions.disprove: Prove some specific order 4k admits no Hadamard matrix. Finitely certifiable in principle (finite search space), but infeasible; a proof would need theory.

problems.title: P versus NP
problems.statement: P is not equal to NP.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical separation between deterministic polynomial time and nondeterministic polynomial time.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving P = NP, for example by giving a polynomial-time SAT algorithm with proofs of correctness and polynomial running time.

problems.title: Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap (Clay problem)
problems.statement: For every compact simple gauge group G, a non-trivial quantum Yang–Mills theory on ℝ⁴ exists at the required axiomatic rigor and has a positive mass gap.

directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by either (a) constructing the rigorous four-dimensional theory and proving that it is gapless, or (b) proving that no theory satisfying the stated axioms exists.

problems.title: The Hodge Conjecture
problems.statement: On a smooth projective complex variety X, every rational cohomology class of type (p, p) is a ℚ-linear combination of classes of algebraic cycles.

directions.disprove: Exhibit a variety and a Hodge class that is not algebraic (the hard part being the proof of non-algebraicity — there is no finite certificate for "not algebraic," so this is proof-required).

problems.title: The Jacobian Conjecture
problems.statement: Every polynomial map F: ℂⁿ → ℂⁿ whose Jacobian determinant is a nonzero constant is invertible (with polynomial inverse).

directions.disprove: Exhibit a non-invertible polynomial map with constant nonzero Jacobian — a finite certificate (the map's coefficients, plus a witness of non-injectivity: two points with equal image, checkable exactly).

problems.title: Kaplansky's Zero-Divisor Conjecture
problems.statement: If G is a torsion-free group and K a field, the group ring K[G] has no zero divisors.

directions.disprove: Exhibit a torsion-free group and two nonzero elements of K[G] with product zero — a finite certificate (finitely supported elements; multiplication checkable in the group).

problems.title: The Smooth 4-Dimensional Poincaré Conjecture
problems.statement: Every smooth 4-manifold homeomorphic to S⁴ is diffeomorphic to S⁴.

directions.disprove: Exhibit an **exotic S⁴** — a smooth manifold homeomorphic but not diffeomorphic to the 4-sphere. The manifold itself can be given by a finite handle/Kirby diagram; the hard part is proving non-diffeomorphism.

problems.title: The Slice-Ribbon Conjecture
problems.statement: Every smoothly slice knot (bounding a smooth disk in the 4-ball) is ribbon (bounding an immersed disk in S³ with only ribbon singularities).

directions.disprove: Exhibit a slice knot that is not ribbon. The knot is a finite object and sliceness can be certified by an explicit disk; the obstruction — proving *non-ribbonness of a slice knot* — is the problem: **no invariant is currently known that can distinguish slice from ribbon**, so this direction awaits a new tool (again a detection limitation, not evidence).

problems.title: The Whitehead Asphericity Conjecture
problems.statement: Every connected subcomplex of an aspherical 2-dimensional CW-complex is aspherical.

directions.disprove: Exhibit an aspherical 2-complex with a non-aspherical subcomplex.

problems.title: Hilbert's 16th Problem (second part)
problems.statement: For every degree n, there is a finite uniform bound H(n) on the number of limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields of degree at most n.

directions.disprove: Prove that for some n there is **no uniform bound** — degree-n systems with arbitrarily many limit cycles. Note the shape of this disproof: Écalle and Ilyashenko proved every *individual* polynomial system has finitely many limit cycles, so no single system is a counterexample; a disproof requires an infinite family with cycle counts → ∞. (Scope of the finiteness theorem: it bounds each system separately, with no uniformity — it is fully consistent with H(n) = ∞ in the uniform sense.)

problems.title: The Casas-Alvero Conjecture
problems.statement: If a complex polynomial f of degree n shares at least one root with each of its derivatives f′, f″, …, f^{(n−1)} (each derivative separately — not necessarily the same root), then f = c(x − a)ⁿ.

directions.disprove: Exhibit one polynomial violating this — a finite certificate in algebraic numbers, exactly verifiable.

problems.title: Vaught's Conjecture
problems.statement: A complete first-order theory in a countable language has either at most countably many or exactly 2^{ℵ₀} non-isomorphic countable models — never an intermediate number.

directions.disprove: Exhibit a theory with an intermediate number of countable models.

problems.title: NP versus P/poly
problems.statement: NP is not contained in P/poly; equivalently, some language in NP has no polynomial-size circuit family.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical statement by establishing a superpolynomial circuit lower bound for an explicit problem in NP.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving NP is contained in P/poly.

problems.title: P versus BPP
problems.statement: P equals BPP; every decision problem with an efficient randomized algorithm also has an efficient deterministic algorithm.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical statement by derandomizing every polynomial-time randomized computation.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving that some language lies in BPP but not in P.

problems.title: Matrix Multiplication Exponent
problems.statement: The exponent of square matrix multiplication is 2; for every ε > 0, two n × n matrices can be multiplied using O(n^{2+ε}) arithmetic operations.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical statement. A strictly improved upper bound on the exponent is meaningful partial progress but does not by itself settle the conjecture.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving an unconditional lower bound ω > 2.

problems.title: Strongly Polynomial Linear Programming
problems.statement: Linear programming admits a strongly polynomial algorithm whose number of arithmetic operations is bounded by a polynomial in the number of variables and constraints, independent of the numerical bit-length of the input.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical statement by constructing and analyzing a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving that no strongly polynomial algorithm for general linear programming exists in the stated model.

problems.title: The Unique Games Conjecture
problems.statement: For every ε, δ > 0, there is an alphabet size k such that it is NP-hard to distinguish Unique Games instances in which at least 1 − ε of the constraints are satisfiable from instances in which at most δ of the constraints are satisfiable.

directions.disprove: Disprove the quantified NP-hardness statement unconditionally. A polynomial-time algorithm alone does not settle the conjecture unless it is accompanied by an unconditional proof that the relevant promise problem is not NP-hard; a conclusion using P ≠ NP or any other unstated assumption is only a conditional result under the catalog review policy.

problems.title: Metric TSP Approximation
problems.statement: Metric traveling salesperson admits a polynomial-time 4/3-approximation algorithm.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical statement by giving a polynomial-time algorithm with approximation ratio at most 4/3.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by proving unconditionally that no polynomial-time 4/3-approximation exists. A lower bound based on P ≠ NP, the Unique Games Conjecture, or another unstated assumption is only a conditional result under the catalog review policy.

problems.title: Dynamic Optimality
problems.statement: Splay trees are dynamically optimal: for every access sequence, their total execution cost is within a constant factor of the cost of the optimal offline binary search tree, up to the standard additive term.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical competitive bound for splay trees.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by constructing a family of access sequences on which the ratio between splay-tree cost and optimal offline cost is unbounded.

problems.title: The Polynomial Hirsch Conjecture
problems.statement: There is a polynomial p such that every d-dimensional polytope with n facets has graph diameter at most p(n, d).

directions.prove: Prove the canonical polynomial diameter bound.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by constructing a family of polytopes whose graph diameters grow superpolynomially in their dimensions and numbers of facets.

problems.title: The Log-Rank Conjecture
problems.statement: There is a constant C such that the deterministic communication complexity of every Boolean sign matrix M is at most O((log rank(M))^C), with rank taken over the real numbers.

directions.prove: Prove the canonical polynomial relationship between deterministic communication complexity and logarithmic rank.
directions.disprove: Disprove the canonical statement by constructing a family of Boolean sign matrices whose deterministic communication complexity is superpolynomial in the logarithm of their ranks.
